title: The Summons
objective: Inciting incident: Edric's legitimate grievance is converted into a secret compact that gives the witches the means to engineer his ruin.
summary: Edric takes the blackthorn token and stolen royal seal and returns to court, beginning the secret compact that lets Huldah shape fate, Ysop arrange the occasion, and Merrin create the witnesses used to destroy him.
continuity_notes: King Alaric stripped Captain Edric Vane of rank for unspecified insubordination, suspended his veterans' arrears, and summoned him to court beneath the eclipse.
Plague has closed the roads and devastated Wyrmwood Moor.
Huldah, Ysop, and Merrin possess records showing diversion of Edric's veterans' pay and a stolen lesser seal of the royal treasury; it is distinct from Alaric's personal signet.
Edric accepts the evidence and seal, agrees not to name the witches, and takes a blood-marked blackthorn token formed as a ring.
Huldah offers her voice, Ysop secures access and timing for the eclipse banquet, and Merrin gathers testimony; Edric mistakes their scheme for political support.
Edric leaves Wyrmwood intending to restore his rank and his soldiers' pay, believing he will surrender the seal once the account is opened.
The blackthorn ring resists removal and leaves a dark, branching mark on Edric's finger.
prose_content:
### Scene 1: Justice on the Moor

By dusk, plague had closed Wyrmwood Moor more thoroughly than Alaric’s law. White cloth marked every door with someone living behind it. At the chapel, someone had cut the bell rope. Captain Edric Vane rode through with a summons in his coat and no rank beneath it.

The war had ended beyond the eastern ridges, though no one had paid for the ending. Edric had learned to distrust peace that left the dead hungry. Then the royal courier found him in a mud camp and read the order aloud: Captain Vane was stripped of command for insubordination and summoned to answer beneath the eclipse.

The message named no order refused, no charge, no witness. Beneath those neat sentences, the pay of his company remained suspended pending review. One seal governed both orders. One had taken his command; the other would finish what disease and battle had begun.

He could recite the courier’s face down to the cracked lower lip. Beyond repair waited the wax, blurred flat where the folded order had rubbed inside his coat, and the paper, worn through against his ribs, warm as a healing bruise.

Wyrmwood lay south of the royal road, between Edric and the capital. Once home, it had turned sour under years of obeying distant orders. He turned toward it anyway. An accusation alone would return to him with interest. He needed proof no superior could dismiss as rank spoken by a rankless man.

Through the bog the mare labored, each step reopening the saddle sore beneath Edric’s left hip. Rain found the seams of his cloak and worked inward until wool, linen, and skin held one cold. Between black pools and low banks of peat, the road climbed.

Before sight came vinegar over rot, wood smoke ground into the soil, and the sweetish decay of thatch abandoned too long. His mouth filled with bile. He had tasted battlefield smoke, hospital wine, and the copper bite of his own blood. All three returned in the moor, mixed without ceremony.

A cottage stood behind the stone wall, its window crossed with white cloth. A moment later, someone coughed inside. The fit ended, and no one came to the door.

At the next crossroad, a rope hung between two posts, iron bells tied along its length. A notice warned that the eastern quarantine road had closed. Beyond it, the royal highway remained open. Mud and distance would cost Edric two days before he reached court.

The tithe barn stood on higher ground, its lichen-edged stone half-wall rising above the thatch. Sheltered there years ago, before the eastern campaign, Edric remembered the moor as merely a place people avoided in winter. He dismounted and put his shoulder against the swollen door.

It gave with a groan.

Inside, three lamps burned. A white-haired woman sat beside the hearth, one eye narrowed. Over a table covered with papers stood a second figure. Between Edric and the exit, a third kept watch. No sigils hung on the walls; no bones marked the beams. By every visible measure, it was a clerk’s office furnished on an economy of unpaid bills, not a witch’s den.

His gaze took the door, high window, knives, and distances. Only after taking inventory did he see the ink on the second figure’s fingers.

> “Captain Vane,” the woman by the hearth said.

His hand found his sword hilt before recognition loosened it.

> “The title has been withdrawn.”

> “Not from memory,” she said.

> “Who are you?”

> “Huldah. That is Ysop. The one at the door is Merrin. We have names, since yours has been traveling through the kingdom on royal paper.”

> “Who told you I would come?”

> “The road told us,” Ysop said. “A wounded man abandons the shortest route when he is not ready to arrive empty-handed.”

The words landed too precisely. Edric studied Ysop until her face offered only patience.

> “You know the summons,” he said.

> “We knew the courier would leave camp before you did,” Huldah said. “We did not make the King angry. We merely waited for his anger to find its way here.”

Merrin had not moved from the door. Huldah pushed a bowl across the table. Barley, salt, and the last pale strands of an onion filled it.

> “Eat,” Huldah said. “Revenge spoils faster than bread.”

> “I did not come for your hospitality.”

> “No. You came because no lawful road remains.”

> “That is not true.”

> “Then refuse the soup and prove it.”

Hunger tightened at the smell. Since dawn, he had eaten nothing, and the journey east had made hunger a dull blade behind his ribs. He took the bowl; the first swallow burned. At the second swallow, he drank on without asking their names again. The body had already voted; pride could only file a minority report.

Huldah watched him over the rim of her own cup.

> “How long have you waited?” he asked.

> “Since before your rank was taken.”

> “Then you expected this.”

> “We expected grief to make a door wherever one had been sealed.”

> “Grief made no door.”

> “It brought you through one.”

The sentence settled into him with parade-ground authority, and Edric resented its fit. Men could choose badly, but mud did not issue orders and call obedience duty.

> “What do you want?”

> “The same thing you do,” Huldah said. “An account.”

Merrin lifted an oilskin packet from beneath a folded cloak and set it between them. The cord around it had been sealed once and opened again. Damp had reached the outer paper; inside, the sheets remained dry. They smelled of cedar, vinegar, and iron-gall ink.

Edric did not reach for them.

> “Your account.”

> “Yours.”

Ysop turned the packet toward him. First came a copy of a war-chest warrant. Beside it lay a ledger kept by the Crown’s private household. Edric knew the paymaster’s cramped hand, the way the seven crossed itself, the habit of scraping a nib clean after every total.

On the third page, his recognition stopped.

Names filled the left margin. Some Edric knew as soldiers; others were widows and children entered beside company numbers. Beside each account, someone had copied the pay released in the paymaster’s careful hand. Then came a second column: sums transferred from garrison arrears into Crown property and private holdings.

The totals matched.

Beside each transfer appeared the same royal seal—the seal that had stripped him.

Under Edric’s thumb lay a line he knew. Beside it ran his own certification, copied from the same roll he had signed after the eastern ridge. The ink was not his; the order of the figures was. Arrears first, expenses second, unexplained sums at the bottom: the paymaster had always placed money where command officers rarely looked.

Someone had looked.

> “This proves diversion,” Edric said. “It does not prove Alaric gave the order.”

> “No,” Huldah said. “Only that the Crown has learned a clean way to starve soldiers without calling it war.”

> “It proves a clerk may have stolen the seal.”

> “Then find the clerk.”

> “Or find the chamber that ordered him.”

> “That is the question you will put before the King.”

> “After I prove where the money went.”

> “Proof is not an objection. It is an object with a name attached.”

She spoke as if authority were grain in a locked store, weighed out to the poor by careful hand.

Edric turned to the final page, where several signatures crowded the lower margin. Some declarations claimed the veterans had never received their pay, though the roll said otherwise.

> “You found these men.”

> “Merrin has a talent for finding what powerful men bury,” Huldah said.

Merrin dipped her chin. Her eyes remained on the names.

> “The ledger can be denied as a clerk’s theft,” Merrin said. “A soldier who has not eaten because the Crown’s seal ordered it is harder to dismiss.”

> “The court will want witnesses.”

> “Then it will have them.”

> “I have veterans. Living ones.”

> “For now,” Merrin said.

Edric looked sharply at her. The answer arrived without apology.

> “Where are they?”

> “Dispersed. Hungry. Obliged to men who can call their silence desertion.”

> “Bring them.”

> “That is a road, not a wish,” Ysop said.

Ysop unfolded a second map across the table, covering the eastern road and the capital beyond it. Quarantine lines crossed the moor in red ink. Beyond them, the palace sat in black squares around a courtyard no larger than a thumbnail.

Ysop placed an iron pin at the western gate.

> “The eclipse banquet is there,” she said. “The King, his chancellor, paymasters, captains, and advisers will all drink beneath one roof.”

> “The summons orders me to attend.”

> “It orders your body to arrive. Court custom may deny your voice.”

> “You expect a disgraced captain to interrupt a feast.”

> “I expect you to carry a treasury seal and enough truth to make refusing you costly.”

Ysop tapped the western gate.

> “The guard changes before the second bell. The servants use the north stair. I have made certain both will be unwatched long enough for a man with a grievance and no rank.”

> “Why?”

> “Because you would arrive otherwise.”

The iron pin looked to Edric like a nail driven through his plan. He expected manipulation. Instead, the map offered a more exact version of the road he had chosen.

> “Who are you?” he asked Ysop. “Not your names. Your office.”

> “I find the hour when locked things are least carefully watched.”

> “That is not an office.”

> “It is at court.”

> “And you, Huldah?”

Huldah turned her cup once between her hands, exposing a white scar around her thumb.

> “At court, kings listen to seers when the sun is swallowed. They remember that the sky does not require their permission.”

> “I need soldiers, not prophecy.”

> “Then you should not have come to a moor where prophecy and starvation share a table.”

> “I need the pay ledger read aloud.”

> “A voice is necessary, even when the mouth belongs to an old woman.”

The offer pleased him. For years he had commanded men whose courage could not protect them and whose loyalty had been priced by clerks. Above such men, a voice kings already feared stood ready to carry an accusation farther than any orderly petition.

He looked at Merrin.

> “And you?”

> “I find the men who remember being paid.”

> “Some of the names on that page are dead.”

> “Their company mates live.”

> “Not all of them.”

> “No,” Merrin said. “But the King has never lacked witnesses to what does not directly concern him.”

Three offers fitted together with the small click of a lock finding its key: a voice for his grievance; an hour when the court’s doors opened; men to testify that paper could not contradict hunger.

Edric distrusted plans more than chance. Chance could be refused; a plan that arrived fitted to his need demanded harder examination. Given such a plan, Edric did not examine it closely enough.

> “The Crown cannot refuse a ledger and a seal without looking corrupt,” he said.

> “The Crown can call both theft,” Huldah replied. “It has used worse materials in the past.”

> “Once the account is opened, the seal returns.”

> “If it can be done honestly.”

> “It will be done honestly.”

> “That is the part your pride requires us not to examine.”

> “My pride has kept men alive.”

> “Your pride has not kept them paid.”

The answer entered below his ribs and stayed there.

Ysop uncovered a second object beneath the map: a treasury seal matrix, blackened with soot, no larger than a folded child’s hand. A crown crossed its face, and transport had left a notch in the lower edge.

Edric knew it before Huldah named it.

Not Alaric’s personal signet, the treasury matrix authorized war-chest payments, released arrears, and sent orders into distant garrisons. Beneath its press, Edric had requisitioned bread and boots and watched clerks work with both hands. His hands did not move now.

> “You stole it.”

> “We removed it from a chest that has not yet been noticed empty,” Ysop said.

> “That is theft.”

> “The ledger is theft. This is the mouth that makes the question public.”

> “A stolen seal cannot make guilt honest.”

> “No. It can make guilt difficult to bury.”

Edric looked from the seal to the copied order. Across both ran the Crown’s device and borrowed authority. Paper looked honest because someone with power had pressed wax to it.

A thief who returned stolen property was still a thief, and so were a clerk who diverted a company’s pay and a king who called the transfer a temporary measure. The difference, Edric thought, was that one man could use the wrong tool to repair the damage it had done.

It was a good argument. It was also the kind a desperate man could mistake for an order.

> “What do you want in return?” he asked.

Huldah placed one finger beside the ledger.

> “The evidence is yours to use. The seal is yours to carry. The account is yours to demand. Our names are ours to keep.”

> “You expect me to conceal a theft.”

> “We expect you to return what the Crown has stolen from men who could not protect themselves.”

> “That is not the same thing.”

> “Not in law. In consequence, it may be.”

> “How long will you keep my silence?”

> “Until the account is heard.”

> “And if the King refuses to hear it?”

> “Then the silence will have had more use than you expected.”

From the folds of her shawl, Huldah withdrew a narrow circlet made from blackthorn. Three thorned lengths had been woven into a ring and bound with dull silver wire. Woven into points, the thorns curved inward, small enough to fit a signet finger. It looked less carved than grown: moor work, fitted to a hand.

> “Your condition?” Edric asked.

> “Wear this when the King asks where the evidence came from.”

> “A thorn is not an oath.”

> “It is quieter.”

> “It is also less durable.”

> “The promise supplies the durability.”

Ysop wrapped the seal in wool; Merrin tied the documents. Neither offered advice. Prepared for every answer except refusal, they made refusal expensive.

Edric pictured his company dispersed along the eastern roads. Under arms because no discharge had come, some remained at their posts. Others walked home without the pay they had earned. Beneath the black he had not yet learned to count, some lay dead.

At court, rank would place him at the back, where obedience closed over him like water.

He slid the blackthorn ring onto his stripped hand.

Silver tightened. A thorn pierced his finger, so slight that for a moment he felt only pressure. Then blood welled in a clean line beneath the binding.

Huldah watched.

> “I will not name you to the King,” he said.

> “Will you name us if asked?”

> “I will not volunteer your names.”

> “A narrow oath.”

> “An honest one.”

> “It may hold.”

> “What do you know of that?”

Huldah’s gaze rested on the blood darkening the thorn.

> “I know that a promise made in blood costs more when the body has been wounded first.”

Pulling at the ring, Edric found the silver bind sunk into swelling skin; the thorn had pierced no visible gap. He drew his glove over the mark and forced his fingers closed around the wrapped seal.

> “I will open the account,” he said. “Then the token comes off.”

> “When the account is opened,” Huldah agreed.

> “I meant it.”

> “That is why we are waiting for the eclipse.”

He tucked the papers against his chest, placing the ledger over his heart and the stolen seal above it. Paper, then metal. A true record and the false mouth that might make it heard.

At the door, he paused.

> “You speak for justice?” he asked.

> “We speak where a lack of voices has cost the most,” Huldah said.

> “That is not an answer.”

> “You will know before the candles gutter.”

Outside, rain loosened the earth beneath the quarantine posts. The royal road climbed eastward between black water and the first pale trunks of birch. Beyond the moor lay the capital, the eclipse, and the court that had made him nothing.

Behind him, Huldah had returned to the hearth. Ysop bent over the palace map. Over fresh sheets, Merrin copied the veterans’ names, leaving room beside each for a statement no soldier had yet given.

Like a campaign council awaiting its commander, they looked ready for orders. Edric did not see that the commander was only the part of the design being kept alive.

Mounted, he turned the mare east. His first clear thought was that he would present the ledger, compel an accounting, restore his company’s pay, then return the seal and leave Alaric with nothing but the dignity of being exposed. Second came the lock: Huldah had been right about its fitting.

Beyond the King’s answer, his mind stopped. Pride supplied the missing order.

At the ford, water rose over the mossed stones and filled the gaps between his boots. Barefingered, he drew off the glove and inspected the ring. The silver binding had sunk beneath the swelling skin. Branching from the puncture, a black mark had already closed at its edges.

Edric pulled once; it held. He left it on.
